blocks.heading: Product life cycle
blocks.text: A product life cycle describes the stages a product passes through from introduction, through growth and maturity, and finally decline. It is a model of sales through time, not a promise of identical timing for every product. Introduction commonly involves low initial sales and awareness-building; growth brings rising sales; maturity involves slower growth or a plateau; decline involves falling sales. In introduction, promotion costs are high, there are few competitors and profit is usually low or negative. In growth, sales and profit rise and competitors start to enter. In maturity, sales peak, competition is strongest, prices may be cut and extension strategies (new markets, new versions or new packaging) may be used. In decline, sales and profit fall and the product may be withdrawn or sold at reduced prices. Development can precede introduction, but sales have not yet begun. Managers can use evidence to consider changes, while recognising a temporary fall does not prove permanent decline.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Tula Bottles observes an established range’s sales flattening after earlier growth. The pattern could suggest maturity, but management should examine competition, availability and actual data before choosing a response.
